draft.title: Factorising polynomials over C
card: The fundamental theorem of algebra says a polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots over C, counting repeated roots as many times as they occur.
So over C every polynomial of degree n factorises fully into n linear factors. If a is a root, then (z − a) is a factor.
Example: z² + 4 has roots 2i and −2i, because (2i)² = −4. So z² + 4 = (z − 2i)(z + 2i).
A repeated root counts each time. In (z − 3)²(z + 1), the root 3 is counted twice, so the polynomial has 3 roots and degree 3.
draft.remember: Degree n means n linear factors over C, one for each root.

a.q: Which is the full factorisation of z² + 9 over C?
a.why: The roots satisfy z² = −9, so z = 3i or z = −3i, giving (z − 3i)(z + 3i). (z − 3)(z + 3) expands to z² − 9, which is a sign error.
a.clue: Solve z² = −9, then write one factor for each root.

b.q: P(z) = (z − 2)³(z + i) is a polynomial. How many roots does it have over C, counting repeats?
b.why: The factor (z − 2) appears three times and (z + i) once, so the roots are counted 3 + 1 = 4. This matches the degree, which is 4. Counting only distinct roots gives 2, which ignores the repeats.
b.clue: Add up the powers on all the linear factors.

problems.detail: "One for each root" could be read as one factor per distinct root. That clashes with the card's point that repeated roots count each time, as in (z − 3)², which has two factors for the root 3. Saying "one for each root, counting repeats" would remove the doubt.
